messages.subject: Re: Line transects os point counts?
parts:
Carlos:

All else being equal, line transect sampling is preferable to point=20
transect sampling if for no other reason than you are gathering data=20
while moving. If there is a reason why you cannot gather data while=20
moving (rugged terrain, being swamped by detections, needing to=20
distinguish calls of multiple species) then you should use point=20
counts. But there are challenges with point counts; namely the number=20
of animals available to be detected by you while at a point is small=20
near to the point and increases as distance from the point increases;=20
even if animals are distributed uniformly in the habitat. This is=20
because of the geometry of a circle (area of a circle increases as the=20
square of the circle radius).

While not a study of raptors, you might consult a paper by Prof. Steve=20
Buckland who applied several sampling methods (including line and point=20
transects) to songbirds Buckland, S.T. 2006. Point transect surveys for=20
songbirds: robust methodologies. /The Auk/ *123*, 345-357.=20
<http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/stb/songbird.pdf>

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Line transects os point counts?
parts:
Adding to Eric's comments, for falcons, you might expect to get bias=20
from movement. Any bias will be greater for point transect sampling=20
than line transect sampling. (One of the assumptions of line transect=20
sampling is that any movement of animals is slow relative to the speed=20
of the observer; point transect sampling assumes no movement.) If most=20
birds are detected in flight, then you'll need a field protocol to deal=20
with this - see the 2001 distance sampling book, e.g. pp198-203.

Note also that 4 lines is inadequate replication to give good estimation=20
of abundance - your variance estimate will be extremely unreliable. You=20
would be better having more shorter lines, spread through the state=20
park. Again, see the 2001 book.

Steve Buckland
